In 2020, computer models predicted that COVID-19 spread in large cities could be better controlled by mass testing, and by then isolating all those who tested positive.
Now, a new study in Science suggests that approach may not be the most effective way to control the pandemic. The researchers found that, in the cities they studied, contact tracing was more effective at controlling the virus.
The study focused on the city of Wuhan, where the pandemic began, and on London. The researchers analyzed the effectiveness of different strategies for containing the virus, using data from both cities.
They found that in Wuhan, contact tracing was more effective than mass testing. In London, the two strategies were equally effective.
The researchers say that the reason contact tracing was more effective in Wuhan is that the city imposed a strict lockdown early in the pandemic, which reduced the number of people who could potentially spread the virus. This made it easier to identify and isolate the people who were infected.
In London, the lockdown was not as strict, so there were more people who could potentially spread the virus. This made it more difficult to identify and isolate the people who were infected.
The researchers say that their findings suggest that contact tracing is a more effective way to control the spread of COVID-19 than mass testing, at least in large cities.
However, they caution that their findings are based on data from only two cities, and that more research is needed to confirm their findings.
The researchers also say that their findings do not mean that mass testing is not useful. Mass testing can be used to identify people who are infected with the virus, even if they are not showing symptoms. This can help to prevent the spread of the virus.
Overall, the new study suggests that contact tracing is a more effective way to control the spread of COVID-19 than mass testing, at least in large cities. However, more research is needed to confirm these findings.

Original title:
Low generalizability of polygenic scores in African populations due to genetic and environmental diversity
Author:
Ruthie Birger
Type:
Text
Genre:

Journal:
Nature
Year:
2022
Language:
English
Abstract:
Polygenic scores, which aggregate genetic variants associated with a trait, are increasingly used in biomedical research. However, their low generalizability across populations is a concern, especially for populations of recent African ancestry. This is due to the genetic and environmental diversity of African populations, which are often underrepresented in genome-wide association studies (GWAS) used to develop polygenic scores. This article discusses the implications of this diversity for the use of polygenic scores in African populations and the need for more inclusive GWAS.

samples.src: Evaluation of Visual and Cytology Screening in Preventing Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia and Cervical Cancer in Namibia
samples.ref: Ukuhlolwa Kokuhlolwa Okubonwayo kanye Ne-Cytology Screening Ekuvimbeleni I-Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia kanye Nomdlavuza Womlomo wesibeletho e-Namibia
samples.hyp:
English text:
The aim of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of visual screening (VS) and cervical cytology screening (Pap smear) in preventing cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or worse (CIN2+) and cervical cancer (CC) in Namibia. The study was a retrospective cohort study of all women who attended the gynecology outpatient clinic at the main referral hospital in Windhoek, Namibia, between 1999 and 2009. The women were followed up for a mean of 5.5 years. At the initial visit, 96% of the women underwent a Pap smear, 60% were offered VS, and 45% accepted it. The incidence density of CIN2+ was 10.2 per 1,000 person-years in the unscreened group, 10.8 per 1,000 person-years in the cytology-screened group, and 10.0 per 1,000 person-years in the visually screened group. The incidence density of CC was 0.3 per 1,000 person-years in the unscreened group, 0.4 per 1,000 person-years in the cytology-screened group, and 0.2 per 1,000 person-years in the visually screened group. The adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) for CIN2+ were 1.04 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.50-2.16) for cytology screening and 0.47 (95% CI, 0.16-1.36) for visual screening. For CC, the adjusted HRs were 1.72 (95% CI, 0.29-9.91) for cytology screening and 0.43 (95% CI, 0.06-3.17) for visual screening. Visual screening was associated with a lower incidence of CIN2+ and CC compared with no screening, whereas cytology screening was not. Visual screening was as effective as cytology screening in preventing CC.

The researchers say that this is a major problem because cervical cancer is highly preventable. Regular screening can detect precancerous lesions before they turn into cancer. And there are effective treatments for precancerous lesions.

The Namibian government has set a goal of eliminating cervical cancer by 2030. But the researchers say that this goal will not be achieved unless more is done to ensure that women are tested and treated for precancerous lesions.
The researchers say that their study is a wake-up call for Namibia and other countries with high rates of cervical cancer. They say that it is time to take action to prevent this disease.

# HPV is a virus that damages the cells of the womb, forming wounds called lesions, which can eventually become cancerous.

## What is HPV?

HPV stands for human papillomavirus. It is a virus that damages the cells of the womb, forming wounds called lesions, which can eventually become cancerous. It is estimated that 27,000 women are diagnosed with cervical cancer each year in sub-Saharan Africa, and 22,000 women die from the disease each year. The good news is that cervical cancer is highly preventable through vaccination and regular screening. Vaccination against HPV is recommended for all girls and boys aged 9 to 14 years. Screening can detect abnormal cells before they become cancerous, and treatment can prevent cervical cancer from developing. There is currently no screening test for other types of HPV-related cancers. However, vaccination can prevent these cancers from developing. The best way to protect yourself from HPV is to get vaccinated and to use condoms during sex. Condoms can reduce the risk of getting HPV, but they cannot eliminate the risk completely. Source: BMC Medical Genomics
Authors: Yen-Ling Chen, Chih-Jian Wei, Chih-Long Lee, Chih-Hung Kao, Chao-Yu Kao, Chih-Hung Kuo, Chien-Shiun Chiu, Chih-Wei Tseng, Chih-Wei Tsao, Sheng-Nan Lu, Chih-Hung Kuo, Sheng-Nan Lu
Summary: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection remains a major public health problem worldwide. Antiviral treatment is the standard of care for patients with chronic hepatitis B (CHB). However, the optimal duration of antiviral treatment and the best choice of drugs remain to be defined. In addition, the development of drug resistance is a major concern during antiviral treatment. In this review, we summarize the current status of CHB treatment and the recent progress in new antiviral agents, including nucleoside/nucleotide analogs (NRTIs), nucleoside/nucleotide analogs with interferon (IFN), and non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs). In addition, we also discuss the potential of immune checkpoint blockade in CHB treatment. We hope that this review can provide a reference for the development of future CHB treatment strategies.

The study, “T cell immunodominance in hepatitis B virus infection is altered in co-infection with HIV,” was published in the journal PLOS Computational Biology.
Led by Dr. Sarah Whittaker at the Walter and Eliza Hall Institute of Medical Research in Australia, the team of researchers used a combination of experimental and computational approaches to understand how the immune system responds to HBV infection.
The researchers focused on a type of immune cell called a cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL), which is known to play a key role in fighting HBV infection. CTLs recognize and kill cells that have been infected with the virus.
The team found that in people infected with only HBV, the CTLs tend to target a specific region of the virus called the immunodominant epitope. However, in people co-infected with both HBV and HIV, the CTLs target a different region of the virus called the subdominant epitope.
This shift in target recognition is thought to be due to the way that HIV infection affects the immune system. HIV infection leads to a decline in the number of CTLs that target the immunodominant epitope, which in turn allows the CTLs targeting the subdominant epitope to become more prominent.
The researchers suggest that this shift in target recognition may actually be beneficial for the immune system. By targeting the subdominant epitope, the CTLs may be able to more effectively eliminate infected cells and control the spread of the virus.

About half of the 181 women in the study had preterm births, and researchers found very high amounts of selenium, copper and zinc.
The researchers also found that women who had preterm births had higher levels of the stress hormone cortisol in their hair than women who delivered full-term babies.
The findings are in the journal Hypertension.
The researchers say this is the first study to look at the hair of pregnant women for signs of high levels of these nutrients and stress.
The women in the study had given birth to their babies in 2014 and 2015 at the University of California, San Francisco, medical center.
The researchers say the hair findings suggest that some women may be taking prenatal vitamins that contain high levels of these nutrients.
The researchers say the high levels of selenium, copper and zinc in the hair of the women who had preterm births could be a sign of preeclampsia, a condition that causes high blood pressure and organ damage in pregnant women.
The women who had preterm births also had higher levels of cortisol in their hair than women who delivered full-term babies.
The researchers say this is the first study to look at the hair of pregnant women for signs of high levels of stress.
The researchers say more studies are needed to confirm their findings.
The lead researcher is Brenda Eskenazi of the University of California, Berkeley.
She reported the findings at the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine meeting in San Francisco. The society is the largest specialty organization for healthcare professionals who care for pregnant women.
Ms. Eskenazi said the next step is to find out if the high levels of these nutrients in the hair of pregnant women are a sign of preeclampsia or other problems.
The U.S. National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences has more about preeclampsia.

English text:
A new study has found that high levels of zinc in the blood may increase the risk of preterm birth by over 6 times. The study, which was conducted by researchers at the University of California, San Francisco, analyzed data from over 1,000 pregnant women in the United States. The researchers found that women who had high levels of zinc in their blood were more likely to give birth prematurely than women who had lower levels of zinc in their blood. The researchers also found that the risk of preterm birth increased as the levels of zinc in the blood increased. The researchers concluded that large amounts of selenium and copper did not play a significant role in causing preterm birth, but that high amounts of zinc increased the risk of preterm birth by over 6 times. The researchers suggest that further research is needed to determine the exact role of zinc in preterm birth. They also suggest that pregnant women should be tested for zinc levels and that zinc supplements may be helpful in preventing preterm birth.

samples.hyp:
This article is more than 5 years old

The Lancet Infectious Diseases
Sepsis deaths could be cut by half with new treatment regime

SummaryDownload PDF

A new treatment regime that includes low-dose heparin and drotrecogin could halve the risk of death from sepsis, according to results of a large randomised trial published in The Lancet today (Sept 12th).

Sepsis is a major cause of death in intensive care units worldwide, but there is no effective treatment. Current management focuses on treating the underlying infection, re-establishing blood flow to vital organs, and providing respiratory and circulatory support. However, up to 50% of patients with severe sepsis die despite these interventions.

Previous attempts to find treatments for sepsis have focused on preventing the blood clotting and inflammation that occur in the disorder. Two drugs that were licensed for this purpose—low-dose heparin and drotrecogin (Xigris, Eli Lilly)—nevertheless came under scrutiny after their use became widespread, as both were associated with increased costs and adverse effects.

In order to assess the effects of these agents in sepsis, Philippe Martin (Hôpitaux de Strasbourg, France) and colleagues conducted a large, multicentre trial involving 1628 patients with severe sepsis admitted to 177 intensive care units in 14 countries. Patients were randomly assigned to receive best local care, best local care plus low-dose heparin, best local care plus drotrecogin, or best local care plus both drugs.

During the study, which lasted 2 years, the researchers found that patients given both heparin and drotrecogin were half as likely to die in hospital compared with those who received neither drug (26·4% vs 32·9%). Diagnosis is challenging, and treatment is protracted and often poorly adhered to. Case-fatality rates remain high, even in high-income countries. Rifampicin is a cornerstone of TBM treatment, but standard doses may not achieve adequate cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) concentrations. Higher doses of oral rifampicin can be used, but drug interactions and gastrointestinal side-effects limit their use. 100 mg dose of rifampicin. The area under the concentration-time curve (AUC) for rifampicin was calculated using the trapezoidal method. The AUC value was then compared with a therapeutic target of 7000 mg · h · L−1. The pharmacokinetic parameters of the 100 mg dose of rifampicin were compared with those of the 600 mg dose reported by others.2,3

Results. Thirty-two patients were included in the study. The AUC value of rifampicin in the 100 mg dose was 4322 mg · h · L−1 (range 2711–6317 mg · h · L−1), which is less than the therapeutic target. The pharmacokinetic parameters of the 100 mg dose of rifampicin were similar to those reported by others for the 600 mg dose.

Conclusion. The AUC value of rifampicin in the 100 mg dose is less than the therapeutic target. The pharmacokinetic parameters of the 100 mg dose are similar to those of the 600 mg dose. Rifampicin doses of less than 600 mg may not achieve therapeutic concentrations in patients with smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis.

The second treatment was a single 1,200mg dose of rifampicin, given as a liquid. The team then compared the two treatments.
The researchers found that the single high dose was as effective as the standard treatment, and patients were more likely to complete the course of treatment when they received the single dose.
The single dose was also better for the patients, as it meant they had to visit a clinic only once, rather than multiple times over a two-month period.
The researchers say that this could be particularly beneficial for patients in rural areas, who have to travel long distances to reach a clinic.
The study was carried out in Bangladesh, and the researchers say that the results are likely to be similar in other low-income countries.
The single dose of rifampicin is also cheaper than the standard treatment, which the researchers say could save health systems millions of dollars each year.
Rifampicin is one of the drugs used to treat TB, and is often the first drug given to patients. It is also used to treat other infections, such as meningitis and leprosy.
The researchers say that the study is the first to show that a single dose of rifampicin is as effective as the standard treatment for TB.
They now hope to carry out a larger study to confirm their results.
The study was carried out in collaboration with researchers from the International Centre for Diarrhoeal Disease Research in Bangladesh, the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, the Centre for Health and Global Development in Bangladesh, and the Centre for Global Health Equity in Kenya.
The research was funded by the Wellcome Trust, the UK Medical Research Council, the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, the Foundation for Innovative New Interventions, the Medical Research Council and International Development Research Centre Joint Fund, the National Institute for Health Research, the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, and the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation.
The findings are published in the journal The Lancet.

Rifampicin is a drug used to treat tuberculosis. The new study shows that the standard dose of the drug is not high enough to kill all the bacteria that cause the disease. This means that the infection can come back, or get worse, in some patients.
The study was carried out by researchers from the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine, St George’s, University of London, the University of Pretoria and the University of Cape Town. The research has been published in the journal Clinical Infectious Diseases.
The researchers looked at the results of 1,400 patients who had been treated for tuberculosis meningitis in South Africa, India and Mozambique. The patients were treated with the standard dose of rifampicin, or a higher dose. The researchers found that the standard dose of rifampicin was not high enough to kill all the bacteria that cause the disease. This means that the infection can come back, or get worse, in some patients.
The researchers then carried out a mathematical modelling study to look at how increasing the dose of rifampicin would affect the bacteria that cause tuberculosis meningitis. They found that increasing the dose of rifampicin would kill more of the bacteria, and reduce the risk of the infection coming back, or getting worse, in patients.
The researchers say that the next step is to carry out a clinical trial to test whether increasing the dose of rifampicin improves the health of patients with tuberculosis meningitis. They say that if the trial is successful, it could save thousands of lives.

They then tested the ability of the biochars to adsorb cadmium, lead and copper from water solutions containing the metals at concentrations of 50, 100 and 150 µg/L.
The results showed that the coconut biochar had the highest adsorption capacity for all three metals, followed by the corn cob biochar and then the rice husk biochar.
The highest adsorption capacities of the biochars were obtained at 150 µg/L for all three metals, and the researchers attributed this to the lower pH of the solution at this concentration, which increases the availability of surface functional groups on the biochar particles to bind with the metals.
They also found that the coconut biochar was the most stable in the presence of natural organic matter, which is often found in real-world water treatment scenarios.
The researchers suggest that biochars could be a useful addition to conventional water treatment processes, particularly in regions where heavy metal contamination is a problem.
They note that the locally produced biochars used in the study could be a sustainable and cost-effective solution for water treatment in rural areas.
The study provides valuable insights into the potential of biochars for heavy metal removal from water, and highlights the importance of considering factors such as metal concentration, biochar type and the presence of natural organic matter when designing water treatment systems that use biochars.
Further research is needed to optimize the use of biochars in water treatment and to evaluate their long-term stability and effectiveness in real-world applications.

samples.src: The Atypical Fibrin Fibre Network in Rheumatoid Arthritis and its Relation to Autoimmunity, Inflammation and Thrombosis
samples.ref: Ama-Atypical Fibrin Fibre Network (izakhi ezingajwayelekile) esifeni samathambo nobudlelwane kokuvuvukaka, i-autoimmunity ne-Thrombosis
samples.hyp:
English text
Zulu translation
The Atypical Fibrin Fibre Network in Rheumatoid Arthritis and its Relation to Autoimmunity, Inflammation and Thrombosis
Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease that is characterised by inflammation of the synovial membrane of the joints. The disease is associated with a high risk of cardiovascular disease, partly due to an increased risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE). The prothrombotic state in RA is partly explained by an increased platelet activation and a procoagulant state of the vessel wall. In addition, an atypical fibrin fibre network has been described in plasma from patients with RA. Fibrin formation was initiated by the sequential addition of thrombin and plasminogen to plasma from patients with and without RA. The fibrin fibres formed in plasma from patients with RA were thicker and more branched than those formed in plasma from healthy individuals. The atypical fibrin fibre network was dependent on dense granule content, as the atypical network was no longer observed when dense granule content was depleted from platelets by botrocetin activation. The atypical network was also dependent on fibrinogen structure, as it was not formed in plasma from patients with dysfibrinogenemia. The atypical network was, however, still formed in plasma from patients with afibrinogenemia. Preincubation of plasma with antibodies against ββ′-interacting peptide (bbIP) also abrogated formation of the atypical network. Together, these results suggest that the atypical network is dependent on the presence of both dense granule content and fibrinogen, and that bbIP is exposed upon activation of platelets and fibrinogen. Since the atypical network was only observed in the presence of thrombin, it will only be formed in situations with high levels of thrombin generation, such as in the presence of procoagulant surfaces or in the stasis zone. Thus, the atypical fibrin network may contribute to thrombus formation in the prothrombotic state in RA.

samples.hyp:
South Africans, New Zealanders trust forecasts about the weather at sea
By Reuters
06:13 (GMT+2) Thu, 03 May 2012
The 29th edition of the two-ocean race, the Volvo Ocean Race, is the world's toughest round-the-world sailing competition. The race, which started in Alicante, Spain, on Oct. 8, 2011, crosses the Atlantic, the Southern Ocean, the Pacific, the Indian Ocean and the return trip across the Atlantic.
AUCKLAND (Reuters) - South Africans and New Zealanders are most likely to trust forecasts about the weather at sea, a survey of 28,000 people in 31 countries showed on Thursday.
The Reuters/Robert F. Smith Poll found that 62 percent of South Africans and 59 percent of New Zealanders trust such forecasts, compared with 46 percent of people in Britain and 44 percent in the United States.
The survey was conducted as the 29th edition of the Volvo Ocean Race, the world's toughest round-the-world sailing competition, gets under way in Alicante, Spain.
The race, which started on October 8, crosses the Atlantic, the Southern Ocean, the Pacific, the Indian Ocean and the return trip across the Atlantic.
"The ocean conditions can be very unforgiving and the safety of the crews is paramount," said Mike Bell, CEO of New Zealand-based weather forecasting company MetLabs, which sponsored the Reuters/Robert F. Smith Poll.
"Perhaps it is not surprising that New Zealand and South Africa top the list of countries where people trust marine forecasts, given the number of sailors from these countries who compete in ocean races."
The poll found that people in some countries are up to three times more likely to trust forecasts for the weather on land than forecasts for the weather at sea.
Forecasts for fog were the least trusted, with only 36 percent of respondents saying they trusted them, followed by forecasts for snow (46 percent), rain (52 percent) and sunny conditions (56 percent).
The survey was conducted between April 23 and April 30. In some countries the survey was conducted online and in others by telephone. The margin of error is between plus or minus 1.78 and 2.1 percentage points.

By Reuters

samples.src: A Participatory Approach to Assessing the Climate-Smartness of Agricultural Interventions:
samples.ref: Indlela yokubamba iqhaza yokuhlola ukukhalipha kwesimo sezulu kokungenelela kwezolimo:

A Participatory Approach to Assessing the Climate-Smartness of Agricultural Interventions
Authors
MetadataShow full item record
Abstract
Climate-smart agriculture (CSA) is a framework for transforming agriculture to be sustainable, productive, and resilient to climate change. Despite the growing popularity of CSA, there is no consensus on how to assess the climate-smartness of agricultural interventions. This paper proposes a participatory approach to assessing the climate-smartness of agricultural interventions. The approach is based on the idea that climate-smartness is a multidimensional concept that includes environmental, economic, and social dimensions. The approach involves four steps: (1) identifying the stakeholders, (2) developing a list of indicators, (3) collecting data, and (4) analyzing the data. The paper illustrates the approach with an example from Burkina Faso. The paper concludes that the proposed approach is a useful tool for assessing the climate-smartness of agricultural interventions.

They then used the 2 lists to come up with a final list of 10 indicators that are both important for food security and adaptation, and that are also used in other agricultural studies. The 10 indicators are: 
1. The percentage of people who are food secure
2. The number of crops grown on a piece of land
3. The amount of land that is used for farming
4. The amount of water used for irrigation
5. The amount of money that farmers spend on seeds and fertilizer
6. The amount of money that farmers receive for their crops
7. The number of days that farmers spend working on their crops
8. The number of days that farmers spend working on other things
9. The number of people in a household

WASHINGTON (AP) — The new coronavirus causing the disease COVID-19 is spreading around the world and scientists are racing to learn more about it.
They are comparing it to related viruses to help find vaccines and treatments. They are sequencing its genetic material to learn how it spreads and kills. They are testing people to learn how many are infected. They are tracking the virus to learn where it might go next.
The World Health Organization says the virus has now spread to 100 countries and regions. It has infected more than 35,000 people and killed more than 1,000. Most of the deaths have been in mainland China, where the outbreak began. But the virus has also spread to more than a dozen other countries, including the United States.
Scientists are trying to answer a number of urgent questions. Do children get sick from it? Can it be spread by someone who has it but doesn’t get sick? How long is a person contagious after becoming infected? How long will the pandemic last? And how deadly is it?
Researchers are using a number of tools to try to answer those questions. Here’s a look at some of the ways scientists are trying to learn more about the virus.
COMPARING IT TO RELATED VIRUSES
Scientists are comparing the new coronavirus to other coronaviruses that have caused disease in humans in the past. They are looking for clues that might help them find treatments and vaccines.
Coronaviruses are a large family of viruses. Some cause only mild respiratory illness. But others have caused more serious diseases, including SARS and MERS.
All of these viruses have similar structures and genetic material. That makes it possible to compare them to each other.

Cardiac Arrhythmias in Patients with COVID-19: A Systematic review and Meta-analysis
Abstract 10655
Background: COVID-19 is a new disease caused by SARS-CoV-2 virus. The main symptoms of this disease are fever, cough, and dyspnea. Cardiac arrhythmias are not common symptoms of COVID-19, but the prevalence of this symptom is increasing. The aim of this study was to evaluate the prevalence of cardiac arrhythmias in patients with COVID-19.
Methods: This systematic review and meta-analysis study was registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) under registration number CRD42020212639. In this study, relevant articles were searched in databases including PubMed, Scopus, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar up to August 2021 using keywords: “Cardiac arrhythmias,” “COVID-19,” “coronavirus,” “systematic review,” and “meta-analysis.” Then, the studies were assessed for eligibility. Finally, 635 articles remained for full-text reading and 18 articles were selected for this review.

Abstract
Introduction: Point of care (POC) tests are an important tool for improving health in
developing countries. However, few studies have explored the barriers to POC test
implementation in these settings.
Objective: To explore the barriers to POC test implementation in developing countries,
with a focus on India and South Africa.
Methods: We searched PubMed, ScienceDirect, and the Web of Science using a selection
of keywords. We also searched the bibliographies of retrieved articles and through contact
with subject experts. We present a narrative synthesis of the retrieved data.
Results: Of 1,434 articles identified, 41 were included. The settings of the included studies
were diverse, with a focus on HIV, malaria, and diabetes in adults and HIV and malaria in

Smit M, Marais F. Towards definitions of critical illness and critical care using concept analysis. S Afr J Clin Nutr. 2013;26(1):21-25. 
Abstract
Background: The terms critical illness and critical care are used extensively in the literature, but are not clearly defined. This can lead to confusion and misinterpretation of the concepts. Purpose: The aim of this article is to contribute to the clarification of the concepts critical illness and critical care. Method: LeSueur’s (1998) concept analysis method was used. The method was followed as described by Walker and Avant (2004). Results: Critical illness is a state of severe physiological dysfunction that is life-threatening and requires the presence of a health care professional. Critical care is the specialised nursing care that is provided to the critically ill patient. Conclusion: The definitions of critical illness and critical care are clarified. The definitions can be used as a basis for further research and to guide clinical practice.
Keywords: 
concept analysis, critical illness, critical care, intensive care, intensive care unit

Concept analysis is a process that explores the meaning of a concept (Chinn & Kramer, 1987; Walker & Avant, 2004). The concept is explored in the literature, and the core defining attributes, model cases, borderline cases, and antonym cases are identified. samples.ref: Amandla Nemikhawulo Yesifundo
samples.hyp:
Strengths and Limitations of the Study

The strengths of this study include the following: (1) the study was conducted in a prospective manner, (2) the sample size was relatively large, (3) the use of a comprehensive and validated questionnaire, (4) the inclusion of a wide range of sociodemographic and clinical variables, and (5) the use of a control group.

The limitations of the study include the following: (1) the cross-sectional design, which limits the ability to establish causal relationships, (2) the reliance on self-reported data, which may be subject to recall bias, (3) the potential for selection bias, as participants were recruited from a specific healthcare facility, (4) the lack of diversity in the sample, which may limit the generalizability of the findings, and (5) the inability to control for all potential confounding variables.

Glossary:
- Prospective: conducted forward in time
- Cross-sectional: data collected at a single point in time
- Recall bias: error in self-reported data due to memory inaccuracies
- Selection bias: error due to non-random sampling
- Confounding variables: factors that may influence the outcome and are not accounted for in the study

In this study researchers identified specific genes that play a role in malaria infections in liver cells, which could lead to new anti-malaria drug targets in future.
Malaria is a mosquito-borne disease caused by parasites from the Plasmodium family. When a malaria-infected mosquito bites a human, the parasites enter the human bloodstream and travel to the liver, where they infect liver cells. The parasites then leave the liver cells and infect red blood cells, causing malaria symptoms such as fever and chills.
The Plasmodium parasites that cause malaria have a complex life cycle, and different stages of the life cycle are vulnerable to different drugs. However, current anti-malaria drugs have limitations, and there is a need for new drug targets to combat drug resistance and improve treatment outcomes.
In this study, researchers used a technique called CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing to systematically knock out individual genes in liver cells and determine which genes are required for Plasmodium parasites to infect liver cells. They identified several genes that are essential for parasite infection, including genes involved in cellular metabolism, protein synthesis, and cell signaling.
The identification of these genes provides new insights into the molecular mechanisms of malaria infection and suggests potential drug targets for future anti-malaria drug development. By targeting these genes, it may be possible to disrupt the life cycle of the Plasmodium parasites and prevent them from infecting liver cells, which could lead to new and more effective anti-malaria drugs.

The malaria parasite is transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito. The parasite is injected into the human bloodstream, where it travels to the liver. The parasite then matures and leaves the liver to infect red blood cells. This causes the red blood cells to burst, releasing more parasites into the bloodstream. This cycle of infection and cell bursting causes the symptoms of malaria, such as fever, chills, and sweating. If left untreated, malaria can lead to severe complications and even death. It is important to seek medical attention and take antimalarial medication if you have traveled to an area where malaria is common and have been exposed to mosquitoes. by
Elisabeth Oppenheimer
South Africa—A new study published in Frontiers in Environmental Science calls for a new approach to conservation in South Africa, one that takes into account the combined effects of invasive species, climate change and human activities.
The study's authors, Dr. Elisabeth Oppenheimer and Dr. Janette Edwards, both from the University of Cape Town's Department of Biological Sciences, say that conservation efforts in South Africa have traditionally focused on single threats to biodiversity, such as invasive species or habitat loss, without considering how these threats interact with each other.
They argue that this approach is no longer sufficient, as the impacts of climate change and human activities are increasingly complex and interconnected.
"Conservation in South Africa has traditionally focused on single threats to biodiversity, such as invasive species or habitat loss, without considering how these threats interact with each other," says Oppenheimer. "This approach is no longer sufficient, as the impacts of climate change and human activities are increasingly complex and interconnected."
The study highlights the need for a more integrated approach to conservation, one that considers the combined effects of multiple threats on biodiversity. The authors suggest that this could involve mapping the combined effects of invasive species, climate change and human activities, and using this information to develop targeted conservation strategies.
They also emphasize the importance of involving local communities in conservation efforts, as they are often the most knowledgeable about the impacts of these threats on their environment.
"Local communities are often the most knowledgeable about the impacts of these threats on their environment, and their involvement in conservation efforts is crucial for the success of any strategy," says Edwards.
The study's authors acknowledge that implementing a more integrated approach to conservation will be challenging, as it will require significant resources and collaboration between different stakeholders. However, they argue that the benefits of such an approach will far outweigh the costs, as it will help to ensure the long-term survival of South Africa's unique biodiversity.

Abstract
Savanna woodlands are important C sinks. In Zambia, they cover about 50% of the land area. However, there is little information on the spatial variability of soil organic matter (SOM) and C in these ecosystems. This study aimed to determine the distribution of SOM and C in the top 10 cm of soil in miombo woodlands in Zambia and to identify the edaphic factors controlling SOM and C. SOM and total organic carbon (TOC) were determined in the top 10 cm of soil at 100 randomly selected sites in miombo woodlands in the Chingwidya Forest Reserve. samples.hyp:
How Ethiopia boosted chickpea production
A farmer picks chickpeas in the Amhara region of Ethiopia. © FAO/Anna Szustarski
13/07/18 10:00
Ethiopia has increased its production of chickpeas, a key source of protein for millions of people, with the help of a new variety of seeds and better access to markets, a farmer says.

In the Amhara region of Ethiopia, Hailemichael Asefa has seen the benefits of a new chickpea variety called ‘Gebissa 302’ that is drought-tolerant and has higher yields than the traditional varieties he used to plant.

“Before, I used to plant the local variety of chickpea, but the harvest was very low,” he told the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO). “Now, I plant Gebissa 302 and I get a much higher yield. I also get to harvest earlier.”

The seeds are distributed by the Agricultural Research Institute of Ethiopia (ARIE), which has been working with FAO to develop the new variety.

“FAO has been supporting us in the multiplication of the seed and in the training of farmers on how to use it,” said Solomon Abebe, the head of ARIE’s Legume Crops Research Division.

The new variety has been a game-changer for Hailemichael, who sells his harvest in the market.

“Previously, the local variety was finished before the market opened, so there was no demand left for it,” he said. “But now, with the new variety, I am able to sell all my harvest.”

Chickpeas are a key source of protein for millions of people in Ethiopia, and the country is the world’s second largest producer of the legume after India.

But production has been hampered by the use of traditional varieties that are vulnerable to drought and have low yields.

The new variety, developed by ARIE with FAO’s support, is drought-tolerant and has yields that are 40 percent higher than the traditional varieties.

It has also been bred to be resistant to a fungal disease called ascochyta blight, which can wipe out entire crops.

The new variety is part of a broader effort by the Ethiopian government to boost production of key crops, including chickpeas, teff (a grain used to make bread), maize and wheat.

The new variant, called Omicron, has since become the dominant strain in many countries. The World Health Organization has declared it a “variant of concern” because it spreads more easily than previous variants and may be more resistant to vaccines.
The emergence of Omicron highlights the importance of genomic surveillance, which involves monitoring the genetic changes in viruses over time. Genomic surveillance can help scientists detect new variants early and understand how they might affect the course of the pandemic.
In this article, we will explore how genomic surveillance works, how it is used to track SARS-CoV-2, and what it can tell us about the future of the pandemic.
What is genomic surveillance?
Genomic surveillance is the process of monitoring the genetic changes in viruses over time. Viruses are constantly mutating, or changing their genetic code, as they replicate. Some mutations have no effect, while others can make the virus more transmissible, more virulent, or more resistant to treatments.
Genomic surveillance involves collecting viral samples, such as swabs or sputum, from infected individuals. The samples are then sent to a laboratory, where scientists extract the viral genetic material and sequence it. Sequencing is the process of determining the order of the nucleotides, or building blocks, that make up the genetic code.
By comparing the genetic sequences of different viral samples, scientists can identify mutations and track how they spread. They can also use phylogenetic analysis, which is the study of evolutionary relationships between organisms, to reconstruct the history of the virus and estimate when and where new variants emerged.
How is genomic surveillance used to track SARS-CoV-2?
Genomic surveillance has been crucial in tracking the evolution and spread of SARS-CoV-2 since the beginning of the pandemic. In the early stages, when the virus was first detected in China, scientists quickly sequenced its genome and shared it with the global scientific community. This allowed researchers in other countries to develop diagnostic tests, vaccines, and treatments based on the viral genetic information.
As the pandemic spread, more and more countries began to conduct genomic surveillance of SARS-CoV-2. Some countries, such as the United Kingdom and Denmark, established large-scale sequencing networks that regularly sample and sequence thousands of viral genomes. Other countries, such as Uganda and South Africa, focused on targeted surveillance of specific populations or regions.

English:
Female genital cutting/mutilation (FGC/M) is a traditional practice that involves the partial or total removal of the external female genitalia for non-medical reasons. It is also referred to as female circumcision, though this term is considered by some to be inappropriate and offensive. FGC/M is practiced in 28 African countries, as well as in parts of the Middle East and Asia, and among migrant communities in Europe and North America. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that about 125 million girls and women worldwide are living with the consequences of FGC/M. The practice is also known by other names, including female genital mutilation (FGM), female genitalia mutilation, female genital surgery, female genital alteration, female genital operation, and female genital injury.

FGC/M is not a single practice, but rather a term that encompasses a range of procedures that vary in type, severity, and health consequences. The four types of FGC/M, as defined by WHO, are:

Type 1: This involves the partial or total removal of the clitoris (the small, sensitive, and protruding part of the external female genitalia) and/or the labia minora (the inner folds of the external female genitalia), with or without removal of the labia majora (the outer folds of the external female genitalia). This is also known as Type I FGC, Type I FGM, Type I female circumcision, and Type I female genital cutting.

Type 2: This involves the partial or total removal of the clitoris and the labia minora, with or without partial or total removal of the labia majora, and narrowing of the vaginal opening through the creation of a covering seal by cutting and repositioning the labia minora, with or without removal of the clitoral hood. This is also known as Type II FGC, Type II FGM, Type II female circumcision, and Type II female genital cutting.

Type 3: This involves the partial or total removal of the external genitalia and then stitching together the remaining inner parts of the vulva, resulting in a small opening. This is also known as Type III FGC, Type III FGM, Type III female circumcision, Type III female genital cutting, infibulation, pharaonic FGM, and pharaonic circumcision.

# To stop female genital mutilation, we first need to understand why it’s happening

Female genital mutilation (FGM) is a harmful practice that involves the partial or complete removal of the external female genitalia. It is most common in parts of Africa, the Middle East and Asia, but it is also practiced in some parts of Europe and the Americas. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that around 200 million girls and women alive today have undergone FGM. The practice is also highly concentrated in some countries, with prevalence rates of 98% in Djibouti, 97% in Egypt, 95% in Eritrea, 93% in Somalia, and 89% in Sudan.

FGM is a violation of human rights and has serious physical and psychological consequences for women and girls. It can lead to severe pain, bleeding, infection, and complications during childbirth. It can also cause long-term physical and psychological problems, including chronic pain, depression, and anxiety. Despite these consequences, FGM continues to be practiced in many parts of the world.

To understand why FGM continues to be practiced, it is important to consider the cultural, social, and economic factors that contribute to the practice. In many communities, FGM is seen as a rite of passage that marks a girl’s transition from childhood to adulthood. It is also seen as a way to control female sexuality and to ensure that girls and women will be good wives and mothers. In some cases, FGM is also seen as a way to protect girls from sexual abuse and to ensure their purity and modesty.

FGM is also often practiced as a way to maintain social status and to avoid shame and stigma. In some communities, families that do not practice FGM may be seen as less traditional or less moral, and may face social ostracism or discrimination. This can create a cycle of fear and shame that makes it difficult for families to break away from the practice.

Economic factors can also play a role in the continuation of FGM. In some communities, FGM is seen as a way to increase a girl’s marriageability and to ensure that she will be able to support her family financially. This can create a situation where families feel pressured to practice FGM in order to secure their daughter’s future.

Researchers say they have found a new way that air pollution can harm people: by making it harder for them to have children.

They studied the effects of air pollution on rats. They found that male rats that breathed air polluted with metals had lower sperm counts and were less able to make the female rats pregnant. The metals came from the wear and tear of engines and brakes. They are released into the air as tiny particles.

The research team led by Dr. Leonardo Di Giovangirolamo at the University of Foggia in Italy, published its findings in the Environmental Research journal.

Di Giovangirolamo said the research was done to better understand how air pollution affects reproduction. He said, “We wanted to understand how air pollution affects reproduction, and we found that it can cause infertility.”

The scientists exposed the rats to air pollution for six hours a day, five days a week, over a three-month period. The air contained metals such as lead, zinc, iron, copper and aluminum. These metals are released into the air when engines and brakes wear down. They are also released during the burning of coal and oil.

The researchers said the metals caused the rats’ bodies to produce more chemicals called reactive oxygen species. These chemicals can damage sperm.

The research team said the study showed that air pollution can affect reproduction in a new way. It is not just that pollution can harm a mother or child during pregnancy. The researchers said the pollution can also harm a father’s ability to father a child.

Homegardens are a traditional form of agroforestry in which a variety of food and culturally important plants are grown under a tree canopy. They are an important source of food, medicine, and other resources for many people in the developing world. However, homegardens are often overlooked in conservation efforts, and their cultural significance is not well understood. This research will help to fill that gap by examining the plant species found in homegardens and their importance to local communities. The results of this research will be used to inform conservation and development efforts in the region.
